rows.selection_reason: No experiments have been completed, so all design choices carry maximum uncertainty. The first experiment must establish a performance floor to interpret all subsequent results. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest possible configuration: PCA is the most basic, well-understood RNA encoder with no learned parameters, singleprofile avoids the added complexity of aggregation, and no image modality is involved. This gives us (1) a clean baseline accuracy/F1 against which every other configuration can be compared, (2) a reference for whether multimodal fusion or more complex encoders actually add value, and (3) a fast, low-risk computation that won't waste budget on a complex setup before we know the system works end-to-end. Under a limited budget, anchoring the search with the simplest baseline maximizes the interpretive value of every future experiment.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: RNA-only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485), the dominant uncertainty is which modality carries the most signal. Config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the cleanest single-variable comparison to config_001, isolating the modality choice while holding profile setting constant. Knowing whether image features alone match, exceed, or fall short of the RNA baseline is the highest-level design decision: it determines whether subsequent budget should focus on RNA encoder refinement, image encoder refinement, or multimodal fusion. Without this anchor, any multimodal result would be uninterpretable (we could not tell whether a gain came from the image, the RNA, or their interaction). ResNet50 is chosen over ViT-L as the first image probe because it is a standard, well-calibrated backbone that gives a clear read on whether spatial image features are informative at all before committing to a larger or more domain-mismatched model.

Evidence: Only two experiments are complete. RNA (pca_n2000, singleprofile) achieves 0.485 accuracy while image (resnet50, singleprofile) is very weak at 0.208, establishing RNA as the dominant modality. Uncertainty: We do not yet know whether aggregating multiple profiles per cell (multiprofile) provides meaningful additional signal over a single profile, and this is a foundational design choice that gates many downstream experiments (all multiprofile and multimodal configurations). What this tests: config_002 changes exactly one variable from config_001—switching from singleprofile to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool)—while keeping the same PCA encoder. This gives a clean single-variable comparison. Why it is the best next experiment: With only 2 data points, reducing uncertainty about the profile-setting axis is critical. If multiprofile+avgpool improves over 0.485, it validates the multiprofile pathway and justifies investing in multiprofile variants with stronger encoders and multimodal fusion. If it does not improve, we avoid wasting budget on the entire multiprofile sub-grid. The minimal change (one variable) makes the result interpretable, and avgpool as the simplest aggregation isolates the profile-count effect from aggregation-complexity effects.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) at 0.591 acc is the clear best so far, showing multiprofile aggregation adds ~10.6% over singleprofile (config_001). Image alone (config_010, 0.208) is very weak, so the RNA pipeline is the primary driver. Uncertainty: We don't yet know whether a more expressive aggregation (transformer) outperforms simple avgpool for combining multiple profiles. This experiment (config_003) is a clean single-variable test of aggregation method, changing only avgpool→transformer while holding everything else identical to config_002. It is the best next use of budget because: (1) it directly extends the strongest configuration, (2) it isolates one design decision so the result is interpretable, (3) the outcome informs every subsequent experiment—both RNA-only and multimodal—by telling us which aggregation to pair with other components, and (4) it avoids prematurely investing in multimodal fusion while the image modality's contribution remains unproven.

Evidence: RNA-only with multiprofile + pca_n2000 + avgpool (config_002, acc=0.591) is the strongest result so far, while image-only with resnet50 (config_010, acc=0.208) is very weak. The critical unresolved question for a multimodal cellular profiling study is whether adding the image modality via fusion provides any complementary signal beyond the already-strong RNA features. config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is the direct multimodal extension of the best RNA-only config, isolating the effect of image addition with the simplest (concat) fusion. This is the highest-information next experiment: if it beats 0.591, it justifies further exploration of fusion strategies and image encoders; if it does not, it tells us to concentrate remaining budget on RNA encoder and aggregation refinements rather than the full 36-config multimodal grid. It is the best use of one experiment because it resolves the single most important design decision (multimodal vs. unimodal) before committing budget to finer-grained variations.

The current best (config_018: multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat; acc=0.619) shows that adding image features to RNA-only multiprofile avgpool (0.591) yields a modest +0.028 gain. The only fusion method tested so far is concat. Config_019 is an identical setup except it uses weighted fusion instead of concat, making it a clean single-variable A/B test against the current best. This directly tests whether the fusion strategy is a meaningful lever or whether concat is already near-optimal. If weighted outperforms concat, it signals that the image contribution can be amplified and justifies further exploration of weighted-fusion variants (e.g., with ViT-L or scvi). If they are comparable, it rules out fusion as a high-priority axis and redirects budget toward RNA encoder or image encoder choices. Under a limited budget, this low-risk, high-information experiment is the most efficient next step because it resolves a binary question that gates multiple downstream decisions.

Evidence: The current best (config_019, acc=0.639) uses pca_n2000 as the RNA encoder in a multimodal, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted-fusion setup. RNA is clearly the dominant signal (RNA-only multiprofile+avgpool=0.591 vs image-only=0.208), and the multimodal gain over RNA-only is modest (~5%), suggesting the RNA representation quality is the primary bottleneck. We have zero data on how learned RNA encoders (scvi_n200, scgpt) compare to PCA. Question tested: Does replacing pca_n2000 with scvi_n200 in the best-performing multimodal configuration improve validation accuracy, i.e., does a learned generative latent representation outperform a linear PCA projection for downstream classification? Why best next experiment: config_031 is a clean single-variable swap (RNA encoder only) against the current champion config_019, making the result directly interpretable. It targets the highest-impact unexplored design axis (RNA encoder) while holding all other settings at their empirically validated best values (multiprofile, avgpool, resnet50, weighted fusion), maximizing information gained per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: The largest single-factor improvement observed so far is the RNA encoder swap from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200 in the multimodal/multiprofile/avgpool/weighted setup (config_019→config_031: +3.9% acc, +2.7% F1). We have zero data on the scgpt encoder. Question: Does scgpt outperform scvi_n200 as the RNA encoder in the currently best configuration? Why this experiment: config_043 is an isolated, controlled comparison against config_031—only the RNA encoder changes. This resolves the highest-uncertainty, highest-impact design choice (RNA encoder) in the context where it matters most. If scgpt wins, we have a new best and a direction to exploit; if it loses, we confirm scvi_n200 is optimal and can redirect remaining budget toward the image encoder (resnet50 vs imagenet_vit_l) or aggregation strategy. Under a limited budget, this single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the most influential factor.

Evidence: The current best configuration (config_031: scvi_n200 + resnet50 + avgpool + weighted, acc=0.678) has been built through systematic elimination: multiprofile > singleprofile, avgpool > transformer, weighted > concat, and scvi_n200 >> pca_n2000 > scgpt. The one major untested dimension in this best configuration is the image encoder—only resnet50 has been used. Question: Does upgrading the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l (a larger, more expressive ViT-L model) further improve multimodal performance? Why this is the best next experiment: config_037 is the minimal, direct extension of the current best, changing only the image encoder while holding all other settings at their empirically validated optima. This isolates the image encoder's contribution under the strongest known RNA/fusion/aggregation stack, giving the cleanest signal on whether a stronger visual backbone is worth the added cost. It is both an exploitation of the proven configuration and an exploration of the highest-impact remaining variable, making it the most informative use of the next budget slot.

The current best configuration (config_037: scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) achieves 0.706 accuracy. The only prior evidence on aggregation (config_002 vs config_003) showed avgpool > transformer by ~7 points, but that was with the weaker pca_n2000 encoder. With the stronger scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l combination, it is unclear whether transformer aggregation could close or reverse that gap. Config_039 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) is a single-variable change from the current best, directly testing whether aggregation strategy matters under the strongest encoder pair. If transformer underperforms, we can confidently lock in avgpool and redirect budget to other axes; if it matches or exceeds avgpool, it opens a new optimization direction. Under a limited budget, resolving this uncertainty with the best-known encoders is more informative than testing a lower-priority axis (e.g., scgpt, which already showed a ~15-point deficit).
